title: Placenta Praevia with Abnormal Adhesion – a Retrospective Study
content: Background: Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) refers to abnormal placental attachment, categorized into accreta, increta, and percreta, with varying severity. The incidence of PAS has risen alongside the increasing rate of cesarean sections. PAS is a significant cause of maternal and fetal complications, including bleeding, preterm birth, and intrauterine growth restriction. Early diagnosis is crucial for management and improving outcomes. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study, conducted at the County Emergency Clinical Hospital "Saint Andrew the Apostle" Constanța, analyzed cases of placenta praevia and PAS from 2018 to 2022. Data were collected from observation sheets and operative protocols, involving 13,841 patients. Placenta praevia and PAS were diagnosed using ultrasound, MRI, and histopathology. Results: Among the 13,841 deliveries, 25 cases of placenta praevia (0.82% incidence) and 17 cases of PAS (0.57% incidence) were identified. Ultrasound demonstrated 96% sensitivity and MRI 96% sensitivity for PAS detection. Of the 17 PAS cases, 3 were diagnosed as placenta increta, and 3 as percreta, with all percreta cases involving bladder invasion. Hysterectomy was the standard surgical treatment. Discussion: Risk factors for PAS included previous cesarean sections (94.1% of PAS cases), smoking, and advanced maternal age. The study confirmed the importance of early imaging and the involvement of a multidisciplinary team in managing PAS, particularly in complex cases involving bladder or rectal involvement. Cesarean section followed by hysterectomy was the preferred surgical approach, and uterine artery embolization (UAE) was considered for reducing hemorrhage risk. Conclusions: Smoking, uterine scars, and uterine fibroids are significant risk factors for placenta praevia with pathological adhesion. Ultrasound and MRI are highly accurate in diagnosing PAS, with histopathology providing definitive confirmation. Multidisciplinary care is essential in managing complex cases, ensuring optimal maternal and fetal outcomes. Surgical treatment involves cesarean section and hysterectomy, with additional interventions for bladder invasion in percreta cases.
